notes.summary: Mensuration is about measuring flat shapes (perimeter and area) and solids (volume and surface area). It gives 2 to 4 questions in Tier 1 and 4 to 6 in Tier 2. Almost every question is one formula plus careful arithmetic, so learn the formula tables below and practise with π = 22/7.

concepts.title: Units and conversions
concepts.body:
Most mistakes in mensuration are unit mistakes. Change every length to one unit before you start.

LengthAreaVolume
1 m = 100 cm1 m2 = 10,000 cm21 m3 = 10,00,000 cm3
1 km = 1000 m1 hectare = 10,000 m21 km2 = 100 hectares
1 litre = 1000 cm31 m3 = 1000 litres1 kilolitre = 1 m3

Areas convert with the square of the length factor, volumes with the cube. For example, 2.5 m3 of water is 2500 litres.

concepts.title: Triangles: area and radii
concepts.body:
What you knowFormula
Base and height known½ × base × height
Three sides a, b, c (Heron)s = (a + b + c)/2, area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c))
Two sides and the angle between them½ ab sin C
Right triangle with legs a, b½ ab, and hypotenuse2 = a2 + b2
Equilateral, side aarea (√3/4)a2, height (√3/2)a, perimeter 3a
Isosceles, equal sides a, base barea (b/4)√(4a2 − b2)

Example: sides 13, 14, 15 give s = 21 and area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84. An isosceles triangle with sides 5, 5, 6 has height 4 and area 12.

Learn these right-triangle triplets: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 7-24-25, 8-15-17, 9-40-41, 20-21-29 and their multiples.

Inradius and circumradius

  • Inradius r = area ÷ s (s is the semi-perimeter). So area = r × s.
  • Circumradius R = abc ÷ (4 × area).
  • Right triangle: R = hypotenuse ÷ 2, and r = (a + b − c)/2 where c is the hypotenuse. For 3-4-5, R = 2.5 and r = 1.
  • Equilateral triangle of side a: R = a/√3, r = a/(2√3), so R = 2r. Height = 3r = (3/2)R. The centroid, incentre, circumcentre and orthocentre are the same point.

Example: for sides 13, 14, 15 (area 84, s = 21), r = 84/21 = 4 and R = (13 × 14 × 15)/(4 × 84) = 8.125.

Example: the circumcentre of an equilateral triangle is 3.2 cm from the base. That distance is r, and the height is 3r = 9.6 cm.

concepts.title: Quadrilaterals
concepts.body:
ShapeAreaPerimeterUseful fact
Rectangle l × blb2(l + b)diagonal √(l2 + b2)
Square, side aa2 = d2/24adiagonal a√2
Parallelogram, sides a, bbase × height = ab sin θ2(a + b)diagonals bisect each other
Rhombus, diagonals d1, d2½ d1d24aside a = ½√(d12 + d22)
Trapezium, parallel sides a, b½ (a + b) × heightsum of sidesheight is the gap between parallel sides
Kite, diagonals d1, d2½ d1d2sum of sidesdiagonals are perpendicular
  • Any quadrilateral: area = ½ × one diagonal × (sum of the perpendiculars on it from the other two corners).
  • Joining the midpoints of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram with half the area. For a rectangle it is a rhombus: a 48 cm2 rectangle gives a 24 cm2 rhombus.
  • If a circle touches all four sides of ABCD, then AB + CD = BC + AD.

Example: a rhombus with diagonals 16 cm and 12 cm has area 96 cm2 and side √(82 + 62) = 10 cm.

concepts.title: Regular polygons and the hexagon
concepts.body:
A regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal. For n sides of length a:

  • Each exterior angle = 360°/n, each interior angle = (n − 2) × 180°/n.
  • Number of diagonals = n(n − 3)/2.
  • Area = (n a2/4) × cot(180°/n).

Regular hexagon: it splits into 6 equilateral triangles of side a. Area = 6 × (√3/4)a2 = (3√3/2)a2. Perimeter 6a. Longest diagonal 2a. Its circumradius equals its side.

Regular octagon: area = 2(1 + √2)a2.

Example: a hexagonal field has area 2400√3 m2. Then (3√3/2)a2 = 2400√3, so a2 = 1600, a = 40 m and the perimeter is 240 m.

concepts.title: Circles, rings and wheels
concepts.body:
ShapePerimeterArea
Circle, radius r2πr = πdπr2 = πd2/4
Semicircleπr + 2rπr2/2
Quadrantπr/2 + 2rπr2/4
Ring, radii R and r2π(R + r) for both edgesπ(R2 − r2) = π(R + r)(R − r)
  • A wheel covers one circumference in one turn. Number of turns = distance ÷ (2πr).
  • With π = 22/7, a semicircle's perimeter is (36/7)r.
  • Square inside a circle of radius r: its diagonal is 2r, so side r√2 and area 2r2. Circle inside a square of side a: radius a/2.
  • Three equal circles of radius r touching each other enclose an area of (√3 − π/2)r2: the equilateral triangle joining the centres minus three 60° sectors.
  • Three points on one straight line have no circle through them; three points not on a line have exactly one.

Example: a wheel of diameter 70 cm has circumference 22/7 × 70 = 220 cm. To cover 1.1 km = 1,10,000 cm it turns 1,10,000 ÷ 220 = 500 times.

concepts.title: Sectors, arcs and segments
concepts.body:
A sector is a slice of a circle cut by two radii with angle θ at the centre. It is θ/360 of the full circle.

  • Arc length l = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Sector area = (θ/360) × πr2 = ½ × l × r.
  • Perimeter of a sector = l + 2r.
  • Minor segment area = sector area − area of the triangle = (θ/360)πr2 − ½r2 sin θ.
  • For θ = 90°: segment = r2(π/4 − ½). For θ = 60°: segment = r2(π/6 − √3/4).
  • Major segment = circle area − minor segment.

A clock's minute hand turns 6° every minute; the hour hand turns 0.5° every minute.

Example: a sector of angle 150° from a circle of diameter 42 cm (r = 21) has area 150/360 × 22/7 × 441 = 577.5 cm2.

concepts.title: Paths and borders
concepts.body:
Path area = bigger shape − smaller shape. For a rectangle l × b and path width w:

SituationArea
Path outside, all round(l + 2w)(b + 2w) − lb = 2w(l + b) + 4w2
Path inside, all roundlb − (l − 2w)(b − 2w) = 2w(l + b) − 4w2
Two cross paths through the middlew(l + b) − w2 (the centre square is counted once)
Circular path outside a circle of radius rπ[(r + w)2 − r2]

Example: a park 120 m × 104 m has a 1 m path inside along the boundary. Path area = 2 × 1 × 224 − 4 = 444 m2. Check: 120 × 104 − 118 × 102 = 12480 − 12036 = 444.

Example: a circular garden of radius 14 m with a 7 m wide path outside: 22/7 × (212 − 142) = 22/7 × 245 = 770 m2.

concepts.title: Cube and cuboid
concepts.body:
SolidVolumeTotal surface areaFour walls (lateral)Longest diagonal
Cuboid l × b × hlbh2(lb + bh + hl)2h(l + b)√(l2 + b2 + h2)
Cube, edge aa36a24a2a√3 (face diagonal a√2)
  • (l + b + h)2 = diagonal2 + total surface area. Use it when the sum of edges and one of the others is given. A cuboid has 12 edges, so the sum of edges is 4(l + b + h).
  • If the three face diagonals at one corner are given, add their squares and halve: that gives l2 + b2 + h2. Subtract each face to find each edge.
  • Number of bricks or small boxes = volume of the big box ÷ volume of one.

Example: a 12 × 4 × 3 cm cuboid has volume 144 cm3, total surface area 2(48 + 12 + 36) = 192 cm2 and diagonal √(144 + 16 + 9) = 13 cm.

concepts.title: Cylinders, solid and hollow
concepts.body:
SolidVolumeCurved surfaceTotal surface
Solid cylinder, radius r, height hπr2h2πrh2πr(r + h)
Hollow cylinder (pipe), radii R and rπh(R2 − r2)2πh(R + r), outer plus inner2πh(R + r) + 2π(R2 − r2)
  • A rectangular sheet rolled along its length l makes a cylinder whose base circumference is l.
  • A roller covers its curved surface area of ground in one turn.
  • An open tank or well has no top: count one base only, or none for a well's walls.

Example: r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm gives volume 22/7 × 49 × 10 = 1540 cm3, curved surface 440 cm2 and total surface 2 × 22/7 × 7 × 17 = 748 cm2.

concepts.title: Cones
concepts.body:
Cone with base radius r, height h and slant height l, where l2 = r2 + h2:

  • Volume = ⅓πr2h (one third of the cylinder with the same base and height).
  • Curved surface = πrl. Total surface = πr(l + r).

Example: r = 7, h = 24 gives l = 25, curved surface 22/7 × 7 × 25 = 550 and volume ⅓ × 22/7 × 49 × 24 = 1232.

Cone from a sector: when a sector of radius L and angle θ is folded, L becomes the slant height and the arc becomes the base circumference, so r = L × θ/360.

concepts.title: Frustums
concepts.body:
A frustum is a cone with its top cut off parallel to the base, like a bucket. Its radii are R and r and its height is h.

  • Slant height l = √(h2 + (R − r)2).
  • Volume = (πh/3)(R2 + r2 + Rr).
  • Curved surface = π(R + r)l. Total surface = π(R + r)l + πR2 + πr2.

Example: a bucket with R = 14, r = 7, h = 6 holds 22/7 × 6/3 × (196 + 49 + 98) = 2156 cm3.

concepts.title: Spheres and hemispheres
concepts.body:
SolidVolumeCurved surfaceTotal surface
Sphere, radius r(4/3)πr34πr24πr2
Hemisphere (solid)(2/3)πr32πr23πr2
Hemispherical bowl (open)(2/3)πr32πr22πr2 inside
Spherical shell, radii R and r(4/3)π(R3 − r3)4πR2 outside-

Example: r = 21 cm gives surface area 4 × 22/7 × 441 = 5544 cm2 and volume 4/3 × 22/7 × 9261 = 38,808 cm3. A solid hemisphere of the same radius has total surface 3 × 22/7 × 441 = 4158 cm2.

When a solid is cut, new flat faces appear. Cutting a sphere into 8 equal pieces gives each piece one eighth of the curved surface plus three quarter-circles.

concepts.title: Prisms, pyramids and the tetrahedron
concepts.body:
SolidVolumeLateral surfaceTotal surface
Right prismbase area × heightbase perimeter × heightlateral + 2 × base area
Right pyramid⅓ × base area × height½ × base perimeter × slant heightlateral + base area
Regular tetrahedron, edge aa3/(6√2) = √2a3/12(3√3/4)a2√3a2
  • Square pyramid with base side a and height h: slant height of a face = √(h2 + (a/2)2).
  • A cylinder is a prism with a circular base; a cone is a pyramid with a circular base. The same two rules work.

Example: a hexagonal prism of side 6 cm and height 10 cm has base (3√3/2) × 36 = 54√3 and volume 540√3 cm3. A pyramid on an equilateral base of side 10 cm with height 24 cm has volume ⅓ × 25√3 × 24 = 200√3 cm3.

concepts.title: Melting, recasting and flowing water
concepts.body:
When a solid is melted and made into new solids, the volume stays the same (unless wastage is given). Surface area usually changes.

  • Number of small solids = volume of big solid ÷ volume of one small solid. Cancel π and fractions before multiplying.
  • Water flowing through a pipe: volume per second = area of the pipe's cross-section × speed of water. Keep units equal (cm and cm/s, or m and m/s).
  • A solid dropped into water raises the level by (volume of solid) ÷ (base area of the container).
  • Earth dug from a well and spread around it: volume dug = area of the ring × height of the platform.

Example: a hemispherical bowl of radius 18 cm is emptied into cylindrical bottles of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. Bottles = (2/3 × 183) ÷ (32 × 6) = 3888 ÷ 54 = 72.

Example: water flows at 2 m/s through a pipe of radius 7 cm. Each second 22/7 × 0.072 × 2 = 0.0308 m3 = 30.8 litres flow out.

Largest solid inside another:

SituationSize of the inner solid
Sphere inside a cube of edge aradius a/2
Cube inside a sphere of radius Rcube diagonal = 2R, so edge 2R/√3
Cylinder or cone inside a cube of edge aradius a/2, height a
Cone cut from a cylindersame r and h, volume one third of the cylinder
Sphere inside a cylinderradius = smaller of r and h/2

Cone, hemisphere and cylinder with the same radius r and height r have volumes in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.

concepts.title: Percent change in dimensions
concepts.body:
Area grows with the square of length; volume grows with the cube.

  • Every length changes by x%: area (or surface area) changes by 2x + x2/100 percent. Use −x for a decrease.
  • Every length changes by x%: volume changes by [(1 + x/100)3 − 1] × 100 percent.
  • Only one dimension changes: the result changes in the same proportion as that dimension's power in the formula. For a cylinder, doubling r and halving h makes the volume 22 × ½ = 2 times.
  • Two similar solids: ratio of surface areas = (ratio of lengths)2, ratio of volumes = (ratio of lengths)3.
Every lengthArea changes byVolume changes by
+10%+21%+33.1%

+50%+125%+237.5%

−10%−19%−27.1%

varieties.name: Triangles
varieties.how: Choose the formula from what is given: base and height, all three sides (Heron), two sides with the angle, or a special triangle. For radii use r = area/s and R = abc/(4 × area).

example.q: The sides of a triangle are 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm. Find its area and its inradius.

varieties.name: Quadrilaterals and polygons
varieties.how: Name the shape, write its area formula, then find the missing side or diagonal. A regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles.

example.q: The area of a field shaped like a regular hexagon is 2400√3 m<sup>2</sup>. What does it cost to fence it at ₹16.80 per metre?

varieties.name: Circles, rings and wheels
varieties.how: Check whether the radius or the diameter is given. For wheels, one turn covers one circumference; divide the distance by the circumference after changing to the same unit.

example.q: A wheel has a diameter of 70 cm. How many turns does it make to cover 1.1 km? (Take π = 22/7)

varieties.name: Sectors and segments
varieties.how: A sector is θ/360 of the circle. For a segment, subtract the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord from the sector.

example.q: A chord of a circle of radius 14 cm makes a right angle at the centre. Find the area of the minor segment. (Take π = 22/7)

varieties.name: Paths and borders
varieties.how: Draw the outer and inner shapes. Path area = outer area − inner area. Note whether the path is inside (subtract 2w from each side) or outside (add 2w).

example.q: A park is 120 m long and 104 m wide. A 1 m wide path runs all round it, inside the park. Find the area of the path.

varieties.name: Cubes and cuboids
varieties.how: Write volume lbh, surface 2(lb + bh + hl) and diagonal √(l<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>2</sup>). If face diagonals are given, set up three equations and add them.

example.q: The diagonals of the three faces meeting at one corner of a cuboid are √5 cm, √10 cm and √13 cm. Find its volume.
steps: l<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> = 5, b<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>2</sup> = 10, h<sup>2</sup> + l<sup>2</sup> = 13
Adding: 2(l<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>2</sup>) = 28, so the sum is 14
l = 2, b = 1, h = 3, so volume = 6 cm<sup>3</sup>

varieties.name: Cylinders
varieties.how: Volume πr<sup>2</sup>h, curved surface 2πrh. For a pipe or hollow cylinder use the difference of the outer and inner circles: πh(R<sup>2</sup> − r<sup>2</sup>).

example.q: A metal pipe is 21 cm long. Its outer radius is 5 cm and inner radius is 2 cm. Find the volume of metal. (Take π = 22/7)

varieties.name: Cones and frustums
varieties.how: Find the missing one of r, h, l with l<sup>2</sup> = r<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>2</sup>. When a sector is folded into a cone, its radius becomes the slant height and its arc becomes the base circumference.

example.q: A sector of angle 216° is cut from a circle of radius 25 cm and folded into a cone. Find the volume of the cone.
steps: Arc = base circumference, so r = 25 × 216/360 = 15 cm

varieties.name: Spheres and hemispheres
varieties.how: Sphere: 4πr<sup>2</sup> and (4/3)πr<sup>3</sup>. Solid hemisphere: 3πr<sup>2</sup> and (2/3)πr<sup>3</sup>. When a sphere is cut, add the new flat faces.

example.q: A sphere of radius 21 cm is cut into 8 equal pieces by three cuts through its centre at right angles to each other. Find the total surface area of one piece. (Take π = 22/7)
steps: Each piece has 3 flat quarter-circles = 3 × 1386/4 = 1039.5 cm<sup>2</sup>

varieties.name: Prisms and pyramids
varieties.how: Prism: volume = base area × height. Pyramid: volume = ⅓ × base area × height; lateral surface = ½ × base perimeter × slant height. Find the slant height with Pythagoras.

example.q: A pyramid has a square base of side 8 cm and a height of 3 cm. Find its total surface area.

varieties.name: Recasting and combined solids
varieties.how: Volume is unchanged when melting or pouring. Set big volume = number × small volume, cancel π and common factors first, then divide.

example.q: A hemispherical bowl of internal radius 18 cm is full of liquid. It is poured into cylindrical bottles of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. How many bottles are needed?

varieties.name: Percent change in dimensions
varieties.how: Area depends on length squared and volume on length cubed. Multiply the factors: a 48% decrease means a factor of 0.52.

example.q: The radius of a sphere is decreased by 48%. By what percent does its surface area decrease?
steps: New surface area = 0.52<sup>2</sup> = 0.2704 of the old

tips: Take π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7, and cancel the 7 before multiplying.
Convert all lengths to one unit first. Remember 1 m<sup>3</sup> = 1000 litres and 1 hectare = 10,000 m<sup>2</sup>.
In recasting questions, write volume ÷ volume as one fraction; π, ⅓ and 4/3 usually cancel.
For percent changes, use 2x + x<sup>2</sup>/100 for area and (1 + x/100)<sup>3</sup> − 1 for volume instead of computing both shapes.
Spot triplets (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 7-24-25, 8-15-17, 20-21-29) for slant heights and diagonals.
A regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles; an equilateral triangle's centre is one third of the height above the base.
traps: Diameter is given but the formula needs the radius. Halve it first.
Curved and total surface area are different. Open objects (bowl, tank without a lid, pipe, well) do not have all faces.
A solid hemisphere has total surface 3πr<sup>2</sup>, but an open bowl has only 2πr<sup>2</sup>.
Do not mix the vertical height and the slant height of cones and pyramids.
A path inside a rectangle subtracts 4w<sup>2</sup>; a path outside adds 4w<sup>2</sup>. Two cross paths overlap in a square of w<sup>2</sup>, counted once.
Area units square and volume units cube: 1 m<sup>2</sup> is 10,000 cm<sup>2</sup>, not 100.

formulas.name: Cuboid
formulas.expr: V = lbh, TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl), d = √(l² + b² + h²)

formulas.name: Cone
formulas.expr: V = ⅓πr²h, CSA = πrl, l = √(r² + h²)

formulas.name: Frustum
formulas.expr: V = (πh/3)(R² + r² + Rr), CSA = π(R + r)l

formulas.name: Prism
formulas.expr: V = base area × h, LSA = base perimeter × h

formulas.name: Pyramid
formulas.expr: V = ⅓ × base area × h, LSA = ½ × base perimeter × slant height

questions.q: What is the area of a circle of radius 7 cm? (Take π = 22/7)
What is the volume of a cube whose edge is 6 cm?
Find the area of a triangle whose sides are 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.
Find the curved surface area of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. (Take π = 22/7)
A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small cones, each of radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are made?
questions.solution:
Volume of sphere = (4/3)π × 63 = 288π.
Volume of one cone = (1/3)π × 32 × 4 = 12π.
Number of cones = 288π / 12π = 24.

questions.q: A rectangular garden 40 m × 30 m has a path 2 m wide running all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?

flashcards.back: √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), s = half perimeter
